why: The Plain English Translation follows the critical editions. The Byzantine text also reads "Jesus Christ" for "Christ Jesus" earlier in the verse (KJV "an apostle of Jesus Christ").

p: The critical editions read ekzētēseis, "speculations"; the Byzantine text has zētēseis, "questions, disputes" (KJV "questions").

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont) and Textus Receptus (KJV: "which minister questions")

why: Ekzētēsis is a rare word, found nowhere else in the New Testament; zētēsis is common in the Pastorals (6:4; 2 Timothy 2:23; Titus 3:9). Copyists were more likely to change the rare word to the familiar one than the other way round.
b: For the KJV's "godly edifying" later in the verse, see the note on "God's plan."

t: "The only God" or "the only wise God"?
p: The KJV reads "the only wise God"; the critical editions have no "wise."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont) and Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The critical editions all leave out "wise." The shorter text is the harder one to explain as a change: a copyist who knew the closing praise of Romans, "to the only wise God" (Romans 16:27), would be likely to add the word here, and much less likely to drop it.
b: The meaning hardly changes: the doxology praises God as the one God either way.

t: "I am telling the truth" or "the truth in Christ"?
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV add "in Christ": "I speak the truth in Christ."

readings.en: I am speaking the truth in Christ
readings.plain: What I say in Christ is true

why: The phrase "in Christ" is found in Romans 9:1, "I tell the truth in Christ. I am not lying," and scribes who knew that verse would easily add it here. The shorter reading is supported by witnesses of every kind, including several of the oldest.
b: Sinaiticus has both readings: its first scribe wrote "in Christ," and a corrector removed it.

p: The critical editions use a stronger compound verb for Eve; the Byzantine text uses the same plain verb as for Adam.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont) and Textus Receptus (KJV: "the woman being deceived")

why: The Plain English Translation follows the critical editions, and its "through and through" renders the prefix ex-. The Byzantine reading makes the verb match "Adam was not fooled" earlier in the verse, the kind of evening-out copyists tended to make.
b: Readers should know that the stress on "through and through" rests on this reading. Paul uses the compound verb of the serpent and Eve in 2 Corinthians 11:3.

p: A few Western witnesses read "This saying is human," perhaps "commonly accepted."

readings.w: Nearly all Greek manuscripts and versions; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort and Tregelles; Byzantine text and Textus Receptus
Claromontanus, original hand (06); Old Latin manuscripts b, d, g, m and mon; Ambrosiaster, some manuscripts known to Jerome, Augustine

why: "Trustworthy" is in almost every witness and matches the formula used four other times in these letters. "Human" is limited to Claromontanus and Latin writers, and it was probably a change made because "This saying is trustworthy" seemed too grand for a remark about church office.
b: There is a second question here: does the formula point back, to 2:15 ("she will be saved"), or forward, to the saying about overseers? Some ancient and modern readers take it with 2:15, since the line about overseers sounds less like a known saying. Most editions and translations take it with 3:1, as the Plain English Translation does.

p: The most famous variant of the letter: ΟΣ ("who") or ΘΣ, the short form of ΘΕΟΣ ("God").

Uncial 061
readings.en: in which (or whom) it was made visible
readings.plain: In whom it was made visible

why: "Who" is in the oldest manuscripts of every kind, in the earliest versions and in fathers from Egypt, Palestine and the West. It is also the harder reading: "who" has no noun to refer back to, since "mystery" is neuter, so scribes improved it either to "which" (agreeing with "mystery") or to "God." In the capital letters of the oldest copies the two words differ by a line or two: ΟΣ "who" and ΘΣ, the usual abbreviation of ΘΕΟΣ, written with a bar above it. A reader could take one for the other, or a corrector could add the strokes.
b: The line most likely begins a hymn about Christ, quoted from the middle, so "who" means "he who," as in Philippians 2:6 and Colossians 1:15, which also begin "who." The Plain English Translation renders it "He." The reading "God" teaches nothing that the New Testament does not say elsewhere (John 1:1, 14), and it is no proof that modern editions deny Christ's divinity: they print "who" because of the manuscripts. Wesley's Notes (1755) still read "God was manifest in the flesh."

p: Two Greek verbs that look alike: agōnizometha, "we struggle," and oneidizometha, "we are insulted."

readings.w: Sinaiticus, original hand (01), Alexandrinus (02), Ephraemi (04), the Greek of 010 and 012, K, Ψ, 33, 104, 1175 and others; NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
Sinaiticus corrected (01), Claromontanus (06), L, 81, 630, 1739 and the Byzantine majority; SBLGNT; Byzantine text and Textus Receptus (KJV: "we both labour and suffer reproach")

why: This is a place where the SBLGNT, this site's base text, differs from NA28 and the Tyndale House edition. The Plain English Translation follows NA28 and THGNT: "struggle" has the support of the older uncials, and it fits the athletic language of 4:7-8 ("train," "exercise") and Paul's pairing of "toil" and "struggle" in Colossians 1:29. "Are insulted" is an easy change of a few letters, and it makes good sense too.

t: "A believing woman" or "any man or woman"?
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV say "if any man or woman that believeth have widows."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
readings.en: if any believing woman has widows

readings.w: Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont) and Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: εἴ τις πιστὸς ἢ πιστὴ ἔχει χήρας
readings.en: if any believing man or believing woman has widows

why: The shorter reading is the harder one: it gives the duty to a woman alone, which surprised later copyists, who widened it to include men (compare 5:4, 8). It probably pictures well-off Christian women who took widows of their family or household into their homes.

why: The command is not in the critical editions. It looks like an addition modeled on 2 Timothy 3:5, which closes a similar list with an order to turn away from such people.

p: The oldest text has a puzzling "because"; later copies smooth it to "and it is certain."

readings.w: Sinaiticus, original hand (01), Alexandrinus (02), 010, 012, 048, 061, 33, 81, 1739, 1881; SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort and Tregelles

Sinaiticus corrected (01), Claromontanus corrected (06), K, L, P, Ψ, 104, 614 and the Byzantine majority; Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont) and Textus Receptus (KJV) (KJV: "and it is certain we can carry nothing out")

why: "Because" is the harder reading: it seems to say that we brought nothing into the world because we cannot take anything out, which is odd logic. Copyists eased it by adding "it is clear" (one, Claromontanus' first hand, has "it is true that"). The oldest manuscripts have the short text.
b: How to make sense of "because": perhaps as "so that," or as the conclusion of a proverb, "we came with nothing, which shows we leave with nothing."

p: The critical editions have the rare praupathia; the Byzantine text has the common praotēs (KJV "meekness").

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont) and Textus Receptus (KJV: "meekness")

why: Praupathia occurs only here in the New Testament, and a copyist would be likely to replace it with the familiar praotēs (Galatians 5:23). The Plain English Translation's "a gentle spirit" tries to keep the -pathia, "feeling," of the rarer word.

t: "Keeps all things alive" or "gives life to all things"?
p: The critical editions read zōogonountos, "preserving alive"; the Byzantine text has zōopoiountos, "making alive" (KJV "quickeneth").

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont) and Textus Receptus (KJV: "who quickeneth all things")

why: The Plain English Translation follows the critical editions. Zōopoieō, "make alive," is Paul's usual word (Romans 4:17; 1 Corinthians 15:22), and a copyist could easily put it in place of the less common verb.
b: Either way, Timothy is charged before the God who holds all life in his hands.

a: the life that is life indeed
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read "that they may lay hold on eternal life."

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort and Tregelles
readings.plain: the life that is life indeed

readings.w: Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont) and Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: The phrase "life indeed" is unusual, and copyists replaced it with the familiar "eternal life" of 6:12. The critical editions keep the unusual phrase. The meaning is close either way, but "life indeed" makes a sharper contrast with the false security of riches.

p: The critical editions end with a plural "you"; the Byzantine text has the singular, and later copies add "Amen."

readings.w: Plural "you": SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House (THGNT), Westcott-Hort and Tregelles. Without "Amen": Sinaiticus, original hand (01), Alexandrinus (02), Claromontanus, original hand (06), 010, 012, 33, 81, 1739 original hand, 1881; Coptic Sahidic; Chrysostom

Singular "you": Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont) and Textus Receptus (KJV: "Grace be with thee. Amen."). With "Amen": Sinaiticus and Claromontanus corrected, K, L, P, Ψ, 104, 1739 corrected and the Byzantine majority; Syriac, Coptic Bohairic

why: The plural is the reading of the critical editions and the harder one: in a letter to one man, the singular is what a copyist would expect. "Amen" is missing from the oldest manuscripts; it is the common liturgical ending, added to many letters in later copies.
b: The Textus Receptus also prints a closing note in Greek, pros Timotheon prōtē egraphē apo Laodikeias: the first letter to Timothy was written from Laodicea, "the chief city of Phrygia Pacatiana." These notes were added by later scribes; they are not part of the letter, and modern editions leave them out.
